title: Ardas before a journey
hook: before travel, exams or new work, Sikhs ask for help in Ardas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas before a meal, and your line: thanks before food. Did you pause before a bite? Today the Ardas walks out the front door with you. Day six hundred forty.

The suitcase is zipped. The car is running in the driveway, or the ride is two minutes away. A student has an exam at nine. Someone is starting a new job on Monday and hasn't slept well all weekend. In many Sikh families, before anyone walks out, there's a moment. Hands fold. A short Ardas is said, sometimes by a grandparent, sometimes by the traveler. Sometimes the family goes to the gurdwara first and asks for the Ardas there. Then, and only then, the door opens.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IS ZIPPED.` → `AN EXAM AT NINE.` → `HANDS FOLD BEFORE THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Every full Ardas already asks for this. Near the end comes the line sarbat de kaaraj raas karne: make everyone's tasks succeed. Kaaraj is a task, a piece of work, an undertaking. Raas means set right, brought to a good end. It's a general request, for everybody. Before a journey, an exam, a wedding, a surgery or a new business, Sikhs make it specific: this trip, this test, this first day. Families sometimes offer karah prashad at the gurdwara so the Ardas can be said there, with the congregation joining in. There's a line in the Guru Granth Sahib that many Sikhs know by heart for exactly these moments. In Sri Rag ki Var, on ang 91, it says, in effect: whatever work you want done, speak of it to the Lord; the True Guru will set it right, and you have His word on it. Notice what this asking is and isn't. It isn't a lucky charm, and it isn't a way to skip the studying. Sikh teaching expects honest effort: you still pack, still prepare, still drive carefully. The Ardas puts the effort and the outcome in the right order. You do the work. You place the result in the hands of the One. And then you go, lighter. There's a practical gift in that, too. Saying a task out loud, before you start, makes you name what you're actually walking into. Half of nerves is not knowing what you're afraid of. A short Ardas makes it plain: this is the road, this is what I hope for, this is in Your hands.
screen: `SARBAT DE KAARAJ RAAS KARNE.` · `NAME THIS TRIP, THIS TEST.` · `SPEAK OF IT TO THE LORD.` · `EFFORT FIRST, OUTCOME GIVEN.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of your very next real task: a call, a drive, a meeting, a page of homework. Picture yourself just before starting it. Now name it, plainly, in one sentence: this is what I'm about to do. Add one more: this is what I hope for. Notice what loosens in you once it's said. If you pray, you can place it before the One in your own words, or simply say Waheguru. If not, let the naming itself be the pause. Then, when the sit ends, begin that task. The bell holds the time.
Ardas before a journey. Before travel, exams, new work, Sikhs name the task in Ardas and ask that it be brought to a good end: kaaraj raas.
Your line: ask before you go. Today, before you leave the house or start something hard, stop at the door for one breath and name what you're walking into. Day six hundred forty.

howItsDone: Before travel, exams, a new job or another undertaking, many Sikhs say a short Ardas at home or ask for one at the gurdwara, sometimes offering karah prashad, asking that the task be brought to a good end.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a task or undertaking; sarbat de kaaraj raas, may everyone's tasks succeed.

trapdoor: what you thought: praying for good luck.
what it means: naming the task before God and asking that it come to a good end, after doing your part.
what a scholar hears: the general petition sarbat de kaaraj raas karne is made particular for each occasion, echoing Sri Rag ki Var's counsel to bring every task to the Lord.
